## Module A — Organization and business ecosystem

Organizational ontology

```
Organization
 ├── EngineManufacturer
 │    └── Simpson
 ├── OEM
 │    ├── Mahindra
 │    └── TAFE
 ├── Supplier
 ├── Dealer
 ├── Distributor
 └── ServicePartner

OrganizationalUnit
 ├── WarrantyDepartment
 ├── ServiceDepartment
 ├── QualityDepartment
 ├── EngineeringDepartment
 ├── ManufacturingDepartment
 └── LogisticsDepartment

Person
 ├── ServiceEngineer
 ├── QualityEngineer
 ├── WarrantyOfficer
 ├── InvestigationEngineer
 ├── QualityManager
 └── OEMServiceRepresentative

OrganizationalRoleAssignment
 ├── EmployeeAssignment
 ├── TicketOwnership
 ├── InvestigationAssignment
 └── ApprovalAssignment
```

Important properties:

| Property             | Description                        |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| organizationId       | Unique organizational identifier   |
| organizationName     | Organization name                  |
| organizationType     | Manufacturer, OEM, supplier, etc.  |
| parentOrganization   | Parent relationship                |
| businessRelationship | Relationship between organizations |
| departmentId         | Organizational unit                |
| personId             | Person identifier                  |
| role                 | Role being played                  |
| validFrom            | Role assignment start              |
| validUntil           | Role assignment end                |
| authorityLevel       | Approval authority                 |

## Module B — Product and engine ontology

Manufacturing domain

This is one of the most important modules because the serial number will eventually connect the entire graph.

```
Product
 └── Engine
      ├── EngineFamily
      ├── EngineModel
      ├── EngineVariant
      ├── EngineConfiguration
      ├── EngineAssembly
      └── EngineInstance

EngineInstance
 ├── EngineSerialNumber
 ├── ManufacturingBatch
 ├── ProductionOrder
 ├── ManufacturingDate
 ├── DispatchRecord
 ├── InstallationRecord
 └── OperationalHistory

EngineAssembly
 ├── CylinderBlock
 ├── CylinderHead
 ├── Crankshaft
 ├── Camshaft
 ├── PistonAssembly
 ├── ConnectingRod
 ├── FuelInjectionSystem
 ├── LubricationSystem
 ├── CoolingSystem
 └── Turbocharger
```

Don't assume these are the complete components of Simpson's engines. The actual bill of materials should drive the component hierarchy.

### Important engine properties

| Property              | Example                         |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| engineSerialNumber    | ENG-100245                      |
| engineModel           | S-450                           |
| engineFamily          | S-Series                        |
| engineVariant         | S-450-D                         |
| manufacturingDate     | 2025-02-15                      |
| manufacturingPlant    | Plant A                         |
| productionBatch       | BATCH-025                       |
| productionOrder       | PO-1001                         |
| dispatchDate          | 2025-02-20                      |
| OEM                   | Mahindra                        |
| installationDate      | 2025-03-01                      |
| currentOperatingHours | 1250                            |
| engineStatus          | Operational / Failed / Replaced |

### Critical relationships

```
EngineInstance INSTANCE_OF EngineModel

EngineInstance BELONGS_TO ManufacturingBatch

EngineInstance MANUFACTURED_AT ManufacturingPlant

EngineInstance SUPPLIED_TO OEM

EngineInstance HAS_COMPONENT EngineComponent

EngineInstance INSTALLED_IN OEMProduct

EngineComponent PART_OF EngineAssembly

EngineInstance HAS_OPERATIONAL_HISTORY OperationalHistory
```

One especially important distinction:

An `EngineModel` is not an `EngineInstance`.

The model describes a class of products. The serial-numbered engine is an actual physical instance.

Your quality analysis must primarily operate at the engine-instance level, while aggregating patterns at model, variant, batch and production-series levels.

documents.text:
## Module C — Complaint and ticket ontology

Business-specific + warranty domain

```
ServiceCase
 └── WarrantyTicket
      ├── ComplaintSubmission
      ├── ComplaintForm
      ├── ComplaintLineItem
      ├── ReportedSymptom
      ├── ReportedFailure
      ├── UsageInformation
      ├── ServiceHistory
      ├── CustomerStatement
      ├── SupportingDocument
      ├── PhotoEvidence
      └── VideoEvidence
```

A complaint is not necessarily a confirmed failure.

This is extremely important.

I would model two distinct branches:

```
ComplaintInformation
 ├── ReportedSymptom
 ├── ReportedFailureMode
 ├── ReportedFailedComponent
 ├── ReportedOperatingHours
 ├── ReportedUsageConditions
 └── ReportedCause

InvestigationInformation
 ├── ObservedSymptom
 ├── ConfirmedFailureMode
 ├── ConfirmedFailedComponent
 ├── VerifiedOperatingHours
 ├── ActualUsageConditions
 └── ConfirmedRootCause
```

This separation allows Simpson to detect discrepancies between what the OEM initially reports and what the engineer subsequently observes.

### Complaint properties

- complaintId
- ticketId
- complaintDate
- OEM
- engineSerialNumber
- engineModel
- reportedOperatingHours
- reportedFailureDate
- reportedFailureLocation
- reportedSymptomCode
- reportedFailureCode
- reportedComponent
- customerDescription
- machineApplication
- loadConditions
- serviceHistory
- lastServiceDate
- previousRepairDetails
- attachments
- complaintSubmissionChannel
- complaintSubmittedBy

### Critical relationship model

```
OEM SUBMITS WarrantyTicket

WarrantyTicket CONCERNS EngineInstance

WarrantyTicket HAS ComplaintSubmission

ComplaintSubmission CONTAINS ReportedSymptom

ComplaintSubmission REPORTS ReportedFailure

ComplaintSubmission SUPPORTED_BY Evidence

WarrantyTicket HAS_STATUS TicketStatus
```

Do not represent a customer allegation as a fact.

Use explicit provenance:

```
reportedBy = OEM representative
verifiedBy = Service engineer
verificationStatus = UNVERIFIED
```

This will become very valuable when you build an AI-based investigation assistant.

warranty blueprint
documents.text:
## Module D — Warranty eligibility ontology

Domain + business-specific

Warranty validation should be its own ontology module.

```
Warranty
 ├── WarrantyContract
 ├── WarrantyPolicy
 ├── WarrantyCoverage
 ├── WarrantyPeriod
 ├── WarrantyEligibility
 ├── WarrantyExclusion
 ├── WarrantyClaim
 ├── WarrantyAssessment
 ├── WarrantyDecision
 └── WarrantySettlement
```

### Eligibility decision inputs

| Input                | Meaning                                           |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Engine serial number | Identifies the engine                             |
| Dispatch date        | Determines warranty commencement where applicable |
| Installation date    | May determine commencement under policy           |
| Warranty period      | Duration of coverage                              |
| Operating hours      | Usage-based warranty limit                        |
| Failure date         | Date on which failure occurred                    |
| Service history      | Whether maintenance conditions were met           |
| Failure category     | Whether the failure is covered                    |
| Exclusion            | Whether a policy exclusion applies                |
| Proof of purchase    | Relevant supporting document                      |

### Warranty decision outcomes

```
WarrantyEligibility
 ├── IN_WARRANTY
 ├── OUT_OF_WARRANTY
 ├── CONDITIONALLY_ELIGIBLE
 ├── REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW
 └── INSUFFICIENT_INFORMATION
```

Don't assume the warranty decision is based only on engine age and operating hours.

Actual policies might include different commencement dates, commercial terms, application-specific limits, service requirements and exclusions.

Model these as explicit policy criteria.

### Relationships

```
EngineInstance COVERED_BY WarrantyContract

WarrantyContract GOVERNED_BY WarrantyPolicy

WarrantyPolicy DEFINES WarrantyCoverage

WarrantyAssessment EVALUATES WarrantyClaim

WarrantyAssessment CONSIDERS WarrantyEvidence

WarrantyDecision RESULTS_FROM WarrantyAssessment

WarrantyDecision APPROVED_UNDER WarrantyPolicy
```

### Example decision rule

```
IF:
  engine is within applicable warranty period
  AND operating hours are within applicable limit
  AND failure is covered
  AND no applicable exclusion exists

THEN:
  eligibility = IN_WARRANTY
```

This is an illustrative rule. Actual Simpson policy takes precedence.

An important design principle: the warranty assessment must preserve the policy version used when the decision was made. Otherwise, you may not be able to reproduce an old decision after a policy changes.

documents.text:
## Module E — Investigation and joint inspection ontology

Field service domain

This module models the investigation itself.

```
Investigation
 ├── InvestigationCase
 ├── InvestigationAssignment
 ├── AssignedEngineer
 ├── JointInspection
 │    ├── PhysicalInspection
 │    └── RemoteInspection
 ├── InspectionSchedule
 ├── InspectionParticipant
 ├── InspectionObservation
 ├── InspectionChecklist
 ├── InspectionMeasurement
 ├── InspectionFinding
 ├── DiagnosticTest
 ├── VideoConference
 ├── InspectionReport
 └── InvestigationConclusion
```

### Joint inspection properties

- inspectionId
- inspectionType
- scheduledDate
- actualStartTime
- actualEndTime
- inspectionLocation
- meetingLink
- assignedServiceEngineer
- OEMRepresentative
- inspectionStatus
- checklistVersion
- observedOperatingHours
- observedSymptoms
- inspectionNotes
- evidenceAttachments
- customerAcknowledgement

### Inspection type

```
InspectionType
 ├── PHYSICAL
 ├── REMOTE_VIDEO
 └── HYBRID
```

### Inspection observations

I strongly recommend treating observations as first-class entities.

For example:

```
Observation-001
 ├── subject: Engine ENG-100245
 ├── observedBy: Engineer-001
 ├── observedDuring: Inspection-001
 ├── observationType: Visual
 ├── finding: Oil leakage near cylinder head
 ├── timestamp: 2026-10-20T10:30:00
 ├── evidence: Video-001
 └── confidence: 0.95
```

That observation is not the same thing as the root cause.

The engineer may observe oil leakage, but further investigation may determine that a gasket manufacturing defect caused it.

Keep the chain:

Observation → Finding → Failure Mechanism → Root Cause

Each transition should be supported by evidence and an authorized conclusion.

failure blueprint
documents.text:
## Module F — Failure analysis ontology

Quality and reliability domain

This is arguably the most intellectually valuable module in the entire system.

You need to distinguish the following concepts:

| Concept             | Meaning                          | Example                          |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Symptom             | What is noticed                  | Engine overheating               |
| Failure mode        | How something fails              | Loss of sealing                  |
| Failed component    | What physically failed           | Cylinder head gasket             |
| Failure mechanism   | Physical process causing failure | Thermal degradation              |
| Root cause          | Underlying reason                | Incorrect material specification |
| Contributing factor | Additional factor                | Excessive operating temperature  |
| Consequence         | Result of failure                | Coolant leakage                  |

### Ontology hierarchy

```
Failure
 ├── EngineFailure
 ├── ComponentFailure
 ├── SystemFailure
 └── OperationalFailure

FailureCharacteristic
 ├── Symptom
 ├── FailureMode
 ├── FailureMechanism
 ├── RootCause
 ├── ContributingFactor
 └── FailureConsequence

FailureClassification
 ├── MechanicalFailure
 ├── ElectricalFailure
 ├── ThermalFailure
 ├── LubricationFailure
 ├── CoolingFailure
 ├── FuelSystemFailure
 └── ManufacturingDefect
```

These classifications are illustrative. Simpson's engineering team must establish its actual failure taxonomy.

### Root cause categories

```
RootCauseCategory
 ├── DesignDefect
 ├── ManufacturingDefect
 ├── MaterialDefect
 ├── AssemblyDefect
 ├── SupplierDefect
 ├── InstallationError
 ├── MaintenanceError
 ├── OperationalMisuse
 └── EnvironmentalCondition
```

You should also allow:

- Multiple contributing factors.
- Multiple possible root causes.
- Root cause not yet determined.
- Root cause rejected after further investigation.
- Root cause confidence and approval status.

A root cause should never be automatically inferred as a confirmed fact simply because an LLM found a similar historical incident.

replacement blueprint
documents.text:
## Module G — Part and engine replacement ontology

Service and logistics domain

There are two distinct workflows.

### G1. Part replacement

```
PartReplacementCase
 ├── FailedPart
 ├── ReplacementPart
 ├── PartAvailability
 ├── ReplacementAuthorization
 ├── PartDispatch
 ├── PartInstallation
 ├── FailedPartReturn
 └── PartReplacementClosure
```

### G2. Engine replacement

```
EngineReplacementCase
 ├── OriginalEngine
 ├── ReplacementEngine
 ├── ReplacementRequest
 ├── ReplacementApproval
 ├── ReplacementCommercialType
 ├── ReplacementDispatch
 ├── EngineRemoval
 ├── EngineInstallation
 ├── FailedEngineReturn
 ├── ReturnShipment
 └── ReplacementClosure
```

### Replacement commercial types

```
ReplacementCommercialType
 ├── WARRANTY_PAID
 ├── GOODWILL
 └── CUSTOMER_PAID
```

Be careful with the term `WARRANTY_PAID`: an SME must establish whether it means a replacement covered by warranty, a cost charged to a warranty account, or another internal commercial arrangement.

### Essential relationships

```
ReplacementCase REPLACES EngineInstance

ReplacementCase AUTHORIZED_BY ReplacementApproval

ReplacementCase HAS_COMMERCIAL_TYPE ReplacementCommercialType

ReplacementCase DISPATCHES ReplacementEngine

ReplacementCase RETURNS FailedEngine

FailedEngine RETURNED_TO Simpson

FailedEngine RECEIVED_BY QualityDepartment
```

### Physical custody and traceability

This is a frequently missed area.

The system should track:

- Which engine was physically removed?
- Which engine was supplied as replacement?
- Who took custody?
- When did the engine leave the OEM?
- When did Simpson receive it?
- Was the seal intact?
- Was there any handling damage?
- Was the engine disassembled?
- Which components were removed?
- Where are the components now?

This requires a separate custody and logistics model, not just a `returned = true` property.

documents.text:
## Module H — Quality assurance and investigation ontology

Quality domain

The returned engine is the source of deeper technical learning.

Model the QA process independently.

```
QualityInvestigation
 ├── ReturnedEngineInspection
 ├── EngineDisassembly
 ├── ComponentInspection
 ├── LaboratoryTest
 ├── MaterialAnalysis
 ├── DimensionalInspection
 ├── MetallurgicalAnalysis
 ├── FailureReproductionTest
 ├── QualityObservation
 ├── RootCauseAnalysis
 ├── InvestigationReport
 └── QualityConclusion
```

### Example QA investigation

```
QualityInvestigation QA-1001

Input:
  Returned Engine ENG-100245

Activities:
  1. Visual inspection
  2. Engine disassembly
  3. Cylinder head inspection
  4. Gasket material analysis
  5. Dimensional verification

Findings:
  - Gasket deformation
  - Abnormal thermal exposure
  - Evidence of coolant leakage

Conclusion:
  Confirmed failure mechanism:
  Gasket sealing degradation

Root cause:
  Pending engineering confirmation
```

The important thing here is that QA can create a technical conclusion that is later used by engineering.

The QA finding is not automatically an engineering change. Those should be separate entities with a formal approval relationship.

capa blueprint
documents.text:
## Module I — Corrective and preventive action ontology

Quality management domain

This module connects failures to organizational learning.

I recommend modeling a CAPA-style structure.

```
QualityIssue
 ├── NonConformance
 ├── FailurePattern
 ├── RootCauseRecord
 ├── CorrectiveAction
 ├── PreventiveAction
 ├── ContainmentAction
 ├── EngineeringChangeRequest
 ├── EngineeringChangeOrder
 ├── ImplementationRecord
 ├── VerificationPlan
 ├── EffectivenessReview
 └── ClosureApproval
```

### Different actions must remain distinct

| Action                     | Purpose                               |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Containment                | Prevent further impact immediately    |
| Correction                 | Fix the specific defective product    |
| Corrective action          | Eliminate the established root cause  |
| Preventive action          | Prevent a potential problem elsewhere |
| Engineering change         | Formalize a technical change          |
| Effectiveness verification | Determine whether the change works    |

### Example

QA finds that a particular gasket specification is associated with repeated overheating failures.

Engineering determines that the material specification must change.

The ontology would capture:

```
QualityIssue QI-1001
    IDENTIFIED_ROOT_CAUSE → RC-1001

RC-1001
    ADDRESSED_BY → CorrectiveAction CA-1001

CA-1001
    IMPLEMENTED_THROUGH → EngineeringChange ECN-1001

ECN-1001
    MODIFIES → GasketSpecification

ECN-1001
    APPLIES_TO → EngineModel S-450
```

This provides a traceable path from an individual failure to a manufacturing-level intervention.

effectivity blueprint
documents.text:
## Module J — Serial-number cut-in and effectivity ontology

Strategically critical module

This is the most important part of your business process to get right.

You mentioned that QA identifies a cut-in number, beyond which the new fix is implemented.

This is not merely a serial number field.

It is a formal concept called Engineering Change Effectivity.

I would model:

```
EngineeringChange
 ├── EngineeringChangeRequest
 ├── EngineeringChangeOrder
 ├── ChangeRevision
 ├── ChangeApplicability
 ├── ChangeEffectivity
 ├── SerialNumberRange
 ├── CutInPoint
 ├── ImplementationDate
 ├── ProductionVerification
 └── EffectivenessMonitoring
```

### Example

Suppose the following is discovered:

| Attribute          | Value                        |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------- |
| Engine model       | S-450                        |
| Quality issue      | Cylinder head gasket failure |
| Corrective action  | New gasket material          |
| Engineering change | ECN-1001                     |
| Cut-in serial      | ENG-100500                   |
| Applicability      | S-450                        |
| Effective from     | 2026-08-01                   |

The change means:

```
ENG-100001 to ENG-100499
    → Previous configuration

ENG-100500 onwards
    → New configuration
```

However, this example assumes that serial numbers are sequential and that the cut-in applies to the entire S-450 series.

In a real production environment, you must validate:

- Is the cut-in per engine model?
- Is it per manufacturing plant?
- Is it per production line?
- Is it per component?
- Is it based on production date?
- Can serial numbers be non-sequential?
- Are there exceptions or retrofits?
- Can multiple changes have different effectivity boundaries?

For example, if the same engine model is manufactured at two plants, a single global serial threshold may be invalid.

A robust model should therefore support a composite effectivity key:

```
EngineeringChange
 ├── EngineModel
 ├── ManufacturingPlant
 ├── ProductionLine
 ├── Component
 ├── SerialNumberRange
 ├── EffectiveDate
 └── ApplicabilityCondition
```

### The recurrence detection logic

Let's say:

- Failure pattern: Cylinder head gasket failure.
- Change: ECN-1001.
- Cut-in serial: ENG-100500.

Now Simpson receives:

| Engine | Serial | Failure        |
| ------ | ------ | -------------- |
| E1     | 100200 | Gasket failure |
| E2     | 100350 | Gasket failure |
| E3     | 100450 | Gasket failure |
| E4     | 100550 | Gasket failure |
| E5     | 100650 | No failure     |
| E6     | 100700 | Gasket failure |

E1, E2 and E3 are pre-cut-in failures.

E4 and E6 are potential post-cut-in recurrences.

But there is an important nuance:

A post-cut-in complaint is not automatically a corrective-action failure.

The system must establish:

1. Does the engine actually fall within the change's applicability?
2. Was the changed component installed?
3. Was the change implemented correctly?
4. Is the new failure mode technically equivalent to the original?
5. Is the root cause the same?
6. Was the engine exposed to sufficient operating hours?
7. Is there a valid inspection or QA conclusion?

Only then should the system classify it as a confirmed post-change recurrence.

This distinction will protect the business from false quality conclusions.

documents.text:
## Module K — Monitoring and reliability ontology

Reliability domain

Once the engineering change is deployed, the work is not finished.

You need a monitoring model.

```
QualityMonitoring
 ├── MonitoringProgram
 ├── MonitoredEnginePopulation
 ├── FailureOccurrence
 ├── RecurrenceEvent
 ├── ReliabilityMetric
 ├── FailureRate
 ├── ExposureMetric
 ├── EffectivenessEvaluation
 ├── MonitoringPeriod
 ├── Alert
 └── MonitoringClosure
```

Some useful metrics:

| Metric                          | What it measures                                  |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Failure count                   | Number of confirmed failures                      |
| Failure rate                    | Failures per defined population or exposure       |
| Post-cut-in recurrence rate     | Confirmed recurrence after engineering change     |
| Mean operating hours to failure | Average usage before failure                      |
| Warranty claim rate             | Warranty claims relative to eligible population   |
| Repeat repair rate              | Repeat repairs for a given engine                 |
| Root cause distribution         | Frequency by root cause                           |
| Change effectiveness            | Whether the corrective action achieved its target |

I would not compare raw failure counts before and after cut-in without accounting for the number of engines and their operating exposure.

For example:

- 5 failures in 100 engines with 1,000 operating hours each.
- 5 failures in 10,000 engines with 100 operating hours each.

These are very different reliability situations.

A proper quality monitoring system needs denominators and exposure data, not just ticket counts.

documents.text:
## Module L — Evidence, document and provenance ontology

Common ontology

This is a cross-cutting module. It should be reused throughout all the other modules.

Every major business assertion should be traceable to evidence.

```
Evidence
 ├── ComplaintEvidence
 ├── InspectionEvidence
 ├── MeasurementEvidence
 ├── PhotographEvidence
 ├── VideoEvidence
 ├── DiagnosticEvidence
 ├── LaboratoryEvidence
 ├── DocumentEvidence
 └── HistoricalRecordEvidence

InformationObject
 ├── ComplaintForm
 ├── ServiceReport
 ├── InspectionReport
 ├── QAReport
 ├── WarrantyApproval
 ├── EngineeringChangeOrder
 └── CorrectiveActionReport

Provenance
 ├── SourceSystem
 ├── SourceRecord
 ├── CreatedBy
 ├── VerifiedBy
 ├── RecordedAt
 ├── ObservedAt
 ├── ValidFrom
 ├── ValidUntil
 └── Revision
```

For example:

```
RootCause RC-1001

SUPPORTED_BY:
  QAReport QA-1001

CONFIRMED_BY:
  QualityEngineer QE-001

CONFIRMED_AT:
  2026-10-25

EVIDENCE:
  - LaboratoryReport LAB-1001
  - Photograph IMG-1001
  - Measurement MES-1001
```

This is how you build a graph that can explain why it believes something.

Do not allow an LLM-generated relationship to become an authoritative relationship without recording its origin and validation status.

Foundational and common architecture
documents.text:
# 2. The five-layer ontology architecture

I recommend separating the ontology into five layers.

## Simpson Enterprise Ontology Stack

## L5 — Business-Specific Ontology

Simpson's warranty policies, failure codes, investigation procedures, goodwill policies, cut-in logic and internal business terminology

## L4 — Organizational Ontology

Simpson organization, OEM relationships, departments, QA teams, engineers, roles, authority and organizational structure

## L3 — Domain Ontology

Engine manufacturing, warranty management, field service, failure analysis, quality management, engineering change management

## L2 — Common / Upper Ontology

Organization, person, asset, product, component, event, process, time, location, document, evidence and decision

## L1 — World / Foundational Ontology

Physical objects, abstract objects, identity, properties, relationships, causality, space, time, change and existence

Higher layers specialize the concepts and semantics defined by lower layers.

Let's examine each layer in detail.

## L1. World / Foundational Ontology

This is the most fundamental layer.

It describes the nature of things that exist in the world, independent of Simpson's business.

You should not create hundreds of Simpson-specific classes here.

Think of it as answering:

- What is an object?
- What is an event?
- What is a property?
- What is a relationship?
- What is an identity?
- What is a physical thing?
- What is an abstract thing?
- What is a process?
- What is a change?
- What is a state?

I recommend using an established foundational ontology as a reference rather than inventing one.

Possible references include:

- BFO (Basic Formal Ontology)
- DOLCE
- UFO (Unified Foundational Ontology)

For an enterprise implementation, you don't need to adopt all of these. Pick one as your foundational reference and use only the distinctions that are useful.

### Foundational concepts

| Class             | Meaning                      | Simpson example                           |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Entity            | Anything that exists         | Engine, engineer, warranty                |
| PhysicalEntity    | Physical object              | Engine, cylinder head                     |
| AbstractEntity    | Nonphysical concept          | Warranty policy                           |
| Object            | Identifiable thing           | Engine assembly                           |
| Process           | An unfolding activity        | Investigation                             |
| Event             | Something that happens       | Engine failure                            |
| State             | Condition of an entity       | Engine operational                        |
| Quality           | An inherent characteristic   | Engine temperature                        |
| Role              | Function played by an entity | Service engineer                          |
| Agent             | Entity capable of action     | Human engineer                            |
| Time              | Temporal reference           | Inspection date                           |
| Place             | Spatial reference            | Customer facility                         |
| InformationObject | Information-bearing object   | Complaint form                            |
| Relationship      | Connection between entities  | Engine supplied to OEM                    |
| Causality         | Cause-effect relationship    | Lubrication failure causes bearing damage |

### Important foundational distinctions

Consider these three things:

1. An engine is a physical object.
2. An engine failure is an event.
3. Engine failure is a category of event.

These must not become the same class.

Similarly:

- A service engineer is a person playing an organizational role.
- An inspection is an activity.
- An inspection report is an information object.
- A failure finding is a conclusion.
- A confirmed root cause is a causal assertion supported by evidence.

These distinctions will prevent serious modeling problems later.

## L2. Common / Upper Ontology

This layer contains reusable enterprise concepts.

These are concepts that would be applicable not just to Simpson, but also to an automobile manufacturer, aircraft manufacturer, industrial machinery company or electronics manufacturer.

Think of this layer as your reusable enterprise vocabulary.

I would define the following common ontology modules.

| Module          | Core classes                                          |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Organization    | Organization, BusinessUnit, Department, Team          |
| Party           | Person, Customer, Supplier, OEM, Partner              |
| Product         | Product, ProductModel, ProductFamily, ProductVariant  |
| Asset           | Asset, Equipment, Component, Assembly                 |
| Event           | BusinessEvent, OperationalEvent, FailureEvent         |
| Process         | BusinessProcess, ProcessInstance, ProcessActivity     |
| Case management | Case, Ticket, Complaint, Claim                        |
| Service         | ServiceRequest, ServiceAssignment, ServiceVisit       |
| Quality         | QualityIssue, Defect, NonConformance                  |
| Document        | Document, Form, Report, Attachment                    |
| Evidence        | Evidence, Observation, Measurement, Photograph, Video |
| Decision        | Decision, DecisionCriterion, DecisionOutcome          |
| Contract        | Contract, Agreement, WarrantyContract                 |
| Time            | DateTime, TimeInterval, EffectivePeriod               |
| Location        | Site, Facility, GeographicLocation                    |
| Inventory       | InventoryItem, StockMovement, Shipment                |
| Finance         | Cost, Payment, Credit, Reimbursement                  |
| Identity        | Identifier, SerialNumber, ReferenceNumber             |
| Change          | ChangeRequest, ChangeAction, ChangeEffectivity        |

### Common ontology relationships

These relationships are reusable:

```
Organization HAS_DEPARTMENT Department

Person PLAYS_ROLE OrganizationalRole

Product HAS_COMPONENT Component

Asset HAS_IDENTIFIER Identifier

Event OCCURS_AT Time

Event OCCURS_AT_LOCATION Location

Process HAS_ACTIVITY Activity

Activity PERFORMED_BY Agent

Case HAS_DOCUMENT Document

Decision BASED_ON Evidence

Decision FOLLOWS_POLICY Policy

Asset HAS_STATE State

ChangeAction HAS_EFFECTIVE_PERIOD TimeInterval
```

One recommendation: define a controlled vocabulary for relationship names.

For example, don't use all of these interchangeably:

```
HAS
BELONGS_TO
RELATED_TO
```
